content: Approximately 13% of women diagnosed with endometrial cancer present with advanced-stage disease, classified as International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stage III or IV. The standard treatment for advanced endometrial cancer typically involves cytoreductive surgery followed by adjuvant therapy, which may include radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination of both. However, there is currently no consensus on which adjuvant treatment approach is the safest and most effective. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of adjuvant chemotherapy compared to radiotherapy or chemoradiation in women with advanced endometrial cancer (FIGO stage III/IV). Additionally, the study aimed to identify which chemotherapy agents or regimens are most effective in this patient population. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Collaborative Review Group's Trial Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to November 2013. They also searched electronic clinical trial registries for ongoing studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing adjuvant chemotherapy with radiotherapy or chemoradiation in women with FIGO stage III or IV endometrial cancer. Four multicenter RCTs involving a total of 1,269 women with primary FIGO stage III/IV endometrial cancer were included in the analysis. All participants had undergone primary cytoreductive surgery. Two trials, involving 620 women (83% with stage III and 17% with stage IV disease), compared adjuvant chemotherapy with adjuvant radiotherapy. Another trial, involving 552 women (88% with stage III and 12% with stage IV disease), compared two chemotherapy regimens: cisplatin/doxorubicin/paclitaxel (CDP) versus cisplatin/doxorubicin (CD), in women who had all received adjuvant radiotherapy. The fourth trial did not contribute data to the analysis. The results showed that overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were significantly longer in women receiving adjuvant chemotherapy compared to those receiving adjuvant radiotherapy. Specifically, the hazard ratio (HR) for OS was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57 to 0.99, I² = 22%), and the HR for PFS was 0.74 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.92, I² = 0%). Sensitivity analyses using adjusted and unadjusted OS data yielded similar results. Subgroup analyses indicated that the survival benefits of chemotherapy were consistent across different stages (III and IV, or IIIA and IIIC), with no significant differences between subgroups (I² = 0%). The quality of this evidence was rated as moderate. One trial provided data on adverse events, showing that women receiving adjuvant chemotherapy were more likely to experience hematological and neurological adverse events, as well as alopecia, compared to those receiving adjuvant radiotherapy. Additionally, treatment discontinuation was more common in the chemotherapy group (33 out of 194 women) than in the radiotherapy group (6 out of 202 women), with a risk ratio (RR) of 5.73 (95% CI 2.45 to 13.36). However, there was no statistically significant difference in treatment-related deaths between the chemotherapy and radiotherapy groups (8 out of 309 versus 5 out of 311; RR 1.67, 95% CI 0.55 to 5.00). In the trial comparing CDP and CD chemotherapy regimens, there was no clear difference in PFS between the two groups (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.17). The quality of this evidence was also rated as moderate. Mature OS data from this trial were not yet available. Severe hematological and neurological adverse events were more frequent in the CDP group compared to the CD group. No trials were identified that directly compared adjuvant chemotherapy with chemoradiation in advanced endometrial cancer. However, one ongoing trial was identified that aims to evaluate this comparison. In conclusion, there is moderate-quality evidence suggesting that adjuvant chemotherapy improves survival by approximately 25% compared to radiotherapy in women with FIGO stage III/IV endometrial cancer. However, chemotherapy is associated with a higher incidence of adverse effects. There is limited evidence regarding whether triplet chemotherapy regimens (e.g., CDP) offer long-term survival benefits over doublet regimens (e.g., CD). Further research is needed to determine the most effective and least toxic chemotherapy regimens and to assess whether the addition of radiotherapy to chemotherapy improves outcomes. A large trial evaluating the benefits and risks of adjuvant chemoradiation versus chemotherapy in advanced endometrial cancer is currently ongoing.
